messages.text:
hello

i’m wondering why the vest padding is 40% poly?

thanks!

cheryl

messages.subject: Re: vest
messages.text:
Hello Cheryl,
 We've tried everything to achieve 100% milkweed in our insulation. And when we say we've tried everything, we mean everything—we are quite tenacious!
 

 However, milkweed fiber simply isn't cohesive and strong enough to be used on its own. Its strength lies in its hollow shape and natural coating, which make it very insulating and waterproof... But it's these same benefits that are also shortcomings in terms of cohesion, mechanical resilience, and therefore, durability. So, we made the imperfect decision to incorporate polyester into our insulators and in the rest of our products, and to maximize two environmental benefits:
 

 1. By offering more durable products, we enable people to keep them longer and buy them less often. This offsets the negative impacts at the beginning of the life cycle, including the use of polyester. There is nothing worse for the environment than a product whose end of life is premature.
 

 2. The undeniable advantage of milkweed is that it can be grown without herbicides, fertilizers, or irrigation, in addition to strongly supporting pollinators, biodiversity, and providing vast habitats for the endangered monarch butterfly.
 

 We believe that the negative impacts associated with the use of synthetic fabrics become more acceptable when considering the many benefits of growing milkweed, which can only be profitable if one is willing to make certain sacrifices to increase the demand for this fiber.
 

 Warmly,
 __
 Gabriel 
 Co-founder 
 Lasclay

messages.text:
thank you for replying and explaining Gabriel. your choice of milkweed is 1000% better than down which is a product of intensive farming of birds and is inherently violent and cruel. 

 with all of the other benefits you mentioned -milkweed is a wonderful natural product!
 

 and, for that matter, the Wuxly winter parka and other vegan outerwear are mostly polyester or other synthetic fabrics. until someone invents a fabric that can replace these synthetics, i’m ok with polyester :). 
 

 warm regards 
 cheryl
